description: In waterlogged land, formerly a lough. This crannog survives as a firm, circular area, approx. 20m diam., surrounded by waterlogged land. title: CRANNOG
description: On level, boggy ground in what was formerly part of Keady Lough, there are now no visible remains of this reported crannog. The landowner reports that some 20-30 years ago he removed a series of axe-sharpened posts from the bog as they were ''getting in the way''. He claims that the posts, which were between 15-30ft in length were arranged to form a circle between 10-15m across & that the posts were driven straight down into the bog. From the description it is clear that this is the site of a crannog. The area of the crannog does seem slightly drier that the surrounding ground but long grass cover at the time of visit made it impossible to determine if the area was in any way raised.

title: CRANNOG
description: In level ground c.1km E of Lough Neagh. The area was a lake, Lough Mooney, drained in the early C19th. The crannog appears as an island green vegetation  which is solid underfoot, in contrast to the surrounding "floating vegetation". The crannog area is 29m N-S x 23m E-W. A drain cuts through the site at NE, but nothing of the crannog structure is visible in section. Below the grass is a dark peaty surface, with horizontal logs, each c.0.1m diam., laid parallel to one another. Below them, at a depth of 0.3m below the surface is a 2nd layer of parallel timbers, at right angles to the upper layer. Worked flint, a rim sherd of coarse pottery, burnt bone, charcoal & burnt clay/daub were all found on the site.

description: In an area of relatively high ground, this lake is located in parkland in the grounds of Quilly House. It is overlooked at NW by a rath (Dow 020:044). The lake seems to be natural, rather than an artifical one associated with the house. It is irregularly shaped & there is an area of marshy ground running off to E. In the lake is one small island far out from any shore. The island is overgrown & the owner''s son, who has been on it a number of times, had never noticed any wooden stakes or crannog features. Considering its overall appearance & situation, however, it is quite likely that this is a crannog.

title: CRANNOG
description: This site is located near the E shore of Lough Macnean Lower, near the mouth of the Arney River. According to the owner of the land around this part of the lough, half of the crannog was drawn away by machines during the 1960s, apparently as part of a process of widening the river mouth. It is possible that the position of the crannog was causing a build-up of silt near the river mouth and perhaps some flooding of the surrounding land. Mr Brady pointed out the remains of the site; some stone piling is visible and some small trees protrude from this. It was impossible to take any accurate measurements at the time of visit.

title: CRANNOG
description: The margins of Drumnavaddy Lake are covered in rushes & sedges & the volume of the lake appears to have diminished slightly. The reported crannog is located on a spur of rushy ground which projects into the lake, giving the lake an almost figure of eight appearance. It was too marshy to approach the site closely, but this would have been an excellent position for a crannog. The ASCD describes it as follows - "The O.S. officers considered that an island in this lake, which had been drained by the 1830''s was artificial. ''It contains one of those islands which may be seen in every lake or marsh which is now dry...This island like all the others has been built probably on piles''".

title: CRANNOG?
description: Situated in Islandderry Lake in an interdrumlin hollow with gently uprising ground all around, especially to the N. and S. On land owned by Islandderry House. The lake is sub-rectangular with its long axis N-S. This small lake still holds a good sheet of water; the edges are marshy and covered in bulrushes, trees and lakeside grasses. The small, circular island is equidistant from the E. and W. shores and slightly nearer to the S-slope than the N. It is small and overgrown with bushes. It has the appearance of being a crannog. This site is described as follows in ASCD (1966), p 184. "The island in this lake may be a crannog site, for W J Knowles is said by the occupants of Islandderry House (relations of his), to have got worked timbers from the site". There are a number of raths in the vicinity; just over the crest of the hill to the N. is DOWN 20:22, though it is not visible from here.

title: CRANNOG?
description: In an inter-drumlin lake, Ardunshin Lough, surrounded on all sides by higher ground with an impressive view of Knockmany to NE. The lake is gradually filling with reeds & bushes & is enclosed by a dense forest. There is now no indication, apart from a circular patch of lilies, of a crannog in this lake. The lilies, which form a circular area c.15m in diam. may indicate slightly shallower water & thus the possible presence of a submerged island.
